title: The Nisaba Mathematics Text
subtitle: An independently written dependency graph, beginning with quantity and growing toward research mathematics.
notationPolicy: Use one symbol for one role whenever practical. Equality is reserved for objects already defined; definitions use :=. Every variable carries an explicit domain. The natural numbers include 0. Subset notation is never ambiguous: ⊆ allows equality and ⊊ means proper subset. Complements name their universe as U∖A. Use · for multiplication and × for Cartesian products. Images and preimages use f[S] and f⁻¹[T]; f⁻¹:B→A denotes an inverse function only when f is bijective. Source-specific aliases are recorded but do not control the main exposition.

chapters.title: Quantities, objects, units, and symbols
chapters.summary: Begin before arithmetic by separating things from attributes, values from units, and mathematical objects from the symbols that name them.
chapters.compressionGoal: Unify the object, measurement, type, equality, and definition language repeated at the start of nearly every mathematical subject.

chapters.title: Matching, counting, place value, and order
chapters.summary: Construct whole numbers from matching and counting, then encode and compare them on a number line.
chapters.compressionGoal: Replace separate counting, numeral, comparison, and place-value units with one construction from correspondence and order.

chapters.title: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication
chapters.summary: Understand arithmetic operations as combining, undoing, repeated grouping, and scaling rather than isolated rules.
chapters.compressionGoal: Give school arithmetic and later algebra one shared operational meaning.

chapters.title: Division, remainders, and divisibility
chapters.summary: Separate sharing, measurement, quotient-with-remainder, and exact divisibility while connecting them by multiplication.
chapters.compressionGoal: Use one quotient-and-remainder model for elementary division, modular arithmetic, algorithms, and number theory.

chapters.title: Signed numbers and distance
chapters.summary: Extend arithmetic to directed change and treat absolute value as distance from zero or between points.
chapters.compressionGoal: Unify debt, temperature, displacement, order, and distance in one number-line model.

chapters.title: Fractions as numbers
chapters.summary: Place fractions on the number line, recognize equivalent forms, and compute by choosing compatible units.
chapters.compressionGoal: Replace separate part-whole tricks with the quotient, scaling, and common-unit ideas reused throughout mathematics.

chapters.title: Decimals, ratios, rates, and percent
chapters.summary: Connect base-ten fractions, relative comparison, unit rates, proportional scaling, and percent.
chapters.compressionGoal: Teach five traditionally separate topics as representations of multiplicative comparison.

chapters.title: Powers, roots, units, and estimation
chapters.summary: Describe repeated scaling, reverse it with roots, and use units and bounds to reject impossible calculations.
chapters.compressionGoal: Join exponentiation, inverse operations, order of magnitude, dimensional analysis, and numerical sanity checks.

chapters.title: Variables, domains, and collections
chapters.summary: Extend the initial symbol language with variable domains, substitution, sets, membership, and extensional equality.
chapters.compressionGoal: Provide one domain-aware collection language used by algebra, logic, formal proof, and computation.

chapters.title: Numbers and algebraic rewriting
chapters.summary: Work with number domains, algebraic laws, equations, and inequalities as meaning-preserving constructions.
chapters.compressionGoal: Replace memorized manipulation rules with a small library of domain-sensitive reversible rewrites.

chapters.title: Statements and logic
chapters.summary: Turn ordinary mathematical claims into precise statements whose truth conditions can be inspected.
chapters.compressionGoal: Use one logical grammar for prose proofs, programs, probability events, and formal verification.

chapters.title: Proof as a checkable construction
chapters.summary: Build direct, case-based, indirect, and inductive arguments from explicit logical goals.
chapters.compressionGoal: Organize proof methods by goal shape and evidence type instead of by textbook tradition.

chapters.title: Sets without notation drift
chapters.summary: Use one stable vocabulary for collections, subsets, and operations that recur throughout mathematics.
chapters.compressionGoal: Create one collection language shared by logic, combinatorics, probability, topology, and algebra.

chapters.title: Functions and composable maps
chapters.summary: Treat functions as typed assignments, then study images, composition, bijections, and inverses.
chapters.compressionGoal: Make typed composition the common interface for formulas, transformations, programs, and morphisms.

chapters.title: Relations and equivalence
chapters.summary: Describe pairwise structure and compress interchangeable objects into equivalence classes.
chapters.compressionGoal: Unify equality-up-to-symmetry, modular congruence, partitions, order, and graph adjacency.

chapters.title: Sequences and recursive construction
chapters.summary: Define an evolving list from initial data and a rule, then reason about every generated stage.
chapters.compressionGoal: Share one state-update language among sequences, induction, algorithms, automata, and dynamical systems.

chapters.title: Algorithms, invariants, and termination
chapters.summary: Specify a process by its state, legal transition, maintained facts, and progress measure.
chapters.compressionGoal: Make algorithm correctness, proof by induction, descent, and state-machine reasoning instances of one pattern.

chapters.title: Finite counting and probability
chapters.summary: Count outcomes without duplication and assign probabilities to explicitly weighted finite experiments.
chapters.compressionGoal: Use the same decomposition of choices for counting, probability, randomized algorithms, and information.

chapters.title: Graphs as relations
chapters.summary: Represent connections by vertices and edges so local relationships produce global paths and components.
chapters.compressionGoal: Give networks, automata, dependencies, molecules, and social connections one discrete relational model.

chapters.title: Vectors and linear systems as computation
chapters.summary: Represent simultaneous constraints with vectors and solve them by reversible elimination.
chapters.compressionGoal: Introduce linear algebra through the common computational core behind equations, geometry, data, and dynamics.

nodes.title: Objects, symbols, and types
nodes.purpose: Read a formula as a sentence about objects instead of as a string of marks.
nodes.motivation: Mathematics talks about numbers, sets, functions, shapes, and many other objects. A symbol is only a name or operation sign; it is not the object itself.
nodes.tutorial:
A **mathematical object** is anything the discussion treats as one thing. A **symbol** is a written name for an object or an instruction. A **type** tells us what sort of object is allowed. The numeral $2$ can name a numerical value, while the word metre names a unit of length. Together, “2 metres” reports a length. Replacing metre by second changes the type from length to duration even though the numeral stays the same.

Before manipulating a formula, ask three questions: What does each symbol name? What type of object is it? What kind of output does each instruction produce?
nodes.keyIdea: Meaning comes before manipulation: every symbol has a role and every operation has an input type.

examples.title: A typed reading
examples.body: In “2 metres,” the numeral 2 names a numerical value and metre names a length unit. Together they report one quantity of type length.

exercise.prompt: In the report “the walk lasted 5 minutes,” identify the object under discussion, the numerical symbol, the unit, and the type of quantity.
hints: Separate the name of the object from the value and unit used to describe it.
Ask which attribute of the walk is being reported.
exercise.solution: The object is the walk, the numerical symbol is 5, the unit is minute, and the reported quantity has type duration.

nodes.title: Equality is not definition
nodes.purpose: Separate a claim that two known objects coincide from the act of introducing a new name.
nodes.motivation: Many books use the same symbol for equality and definition. That saves ink but hides whether a line makes a claim or creates terminology.
nodes.tutorial:
Write $a=b$ when $a$ and $b$ already have meanings and you assert that they are the same object. Write $c:=a$ when you introduce $c$ as a new name for the object already named by $a$. A definition is not proved; later claims using it may need proof.

Equality is symmetric: from $a=b$ we also have $b=a$. Definition has a reading direction: $c:=a$ introduces $c$; reversing the typography would misdescribe what is new.
nodes.keyIdea: Use $=$ for sameness and $:=$ for a new name.

examples.title: Name, then claim
examples.body: Define $h:=$ the height of a particular door. The later line $h=2$ metres is a measured claim, not another definition.

exercise.prompt: Choose $=$ or $:=$ in each blank: (a) introduce $w$ as the width of a page; (b) state that the measured width $w$ is 21 centimetres.
hints: Ask whether the line creates a name or makes a claim.
exercise.solution: (a) $w:=$ the width of the page. (b) $w=21$ centimetres.

sourceRefs.note: Definitions and mathematical statements.

nodes.title: Variables, domains, and substitution
nodes.purpose: Know what values a variable may take and when replacing it preserves meaning.
nodes.motivation: A formula containing $x$ is incomplete until we know which objects $x$ is allowed to represent.
nodes.tutorial:
A **variable** is a symbol whose value may vary. Its **domain** is the collection of allowed values. Substitution replaces a variable by one allowed object everywhere that variable has the same role. For example, if $x$ is a whole number, substituting $x=2$ into $x+1$ produces $2+1$.

The domain can change whether a solution is allowed. The equation $x+1=3$ has the whole-number solution $x=2$, but it has no solution if the permitted values are only 0 and 1. NisabaDB therefore declares a domain when a variable first appears and never relies on the reader to guess it.
nodes.keyIdea: A variable without a domain is an unfinished instruction.

examples.title: A domain changes the answer
examples.body: If $x$ may be any whole number, $x+2=5$ has the solution $x=3$. If only 0, 1, and 2 are permitted, the same equation has no allowed solution.

exercise.prompt: Compare the solutions of $x+2=4$ when the allowed values are all whole numbers and when the allowed values are only 0 and 1.
hints: Substitute the value that makes the left side equal 4, then check whether the domain allows it.
exercise.solution: The equation requires $x=2$. It is a solution in the domain of all whole numbers. It is not allowed when the domain contains only 0 and 1, so that restricted problem has no solution.

sourceRefs.note: Variables, expressions, and solution domains.

nodes.title: Sets, elements, and extensionality
nodes.purpose: Describe a collection by exactly which objects belong to it, without importing a new set-theory introduction in every subject.
nodes.motivation: Sets are the common container language of modern mathematics. The same small core should be learned once and reused everywhere.
nodes.tutorial:
A **set** is determined by which objects are its **elements**. Write $x \in A$ when $x$ is an element of $A$, and $x \notin A$ otherwise. Order and repetition do not change a set: $\{1,2,2\}=\{2,1\}$.

**Extensionality** is the equality rule for sets: two sets are equal exactly when they have the same elements. This gives a standard proof method later—take an arbitrary object and compare membership in the two sets.
nodes.keyIdea: A set has no hidden order or duplicates; its identity is exactly its membership condition.

examples.title: Different lists, one set
examples.body: $A:=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B:=\{3,2,1,1\}$ are equal because every object belongs to $A$ exactly when it belongs to $B$.

exercise.prompt: Are $\{0,1\}$ and $\{0,1,0\}$ equal? Explain using membership rather than list length.
hints: Check which distinct objects belong to each set.
exercise.solution: Yes. Both sets have exactly the elements 0 and 1; repetition in a roster does not create a new element.

sourceRefs.note: Sets and membership as introductory mathematical language.

nodes.title: Number domains and order
nodes.purpose: Use one explicit nesting of familiar number systems and one convention for natural numbers.
nodes.motivation: Authors disagree about whether 0 is natural. Unmarked disagreement causes false edge cases, especially in induction and counting.
nodes.tutorial:
NisabaDB fixes $\mathbb N:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. The integers $\mathbb Z$ add negative whole numbers. The rationals $\mathbb Q$ are fractions of integers with nonzero denominator. The reals $\mathbb R$ include limits such as $\sqrt2$. Thus

$$\mathbb N \subseteq \mathbb Z \subseteq \mathbb Q \subseteq \mathbb R.$$

The symbols $<$ and $\le$ describe order. Writing $a<b$ is a statement; it is not an instruction to move symbols across an inequality.
nodes.keyIdea: Always name the number domain, and always state whether the natural numbers include 0.

examples.title: One number, several domains
examples.body: $3$ belongs to all four displayed domains. $-3$ belongs to $\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q,\mathbb R$ but not $\mathbb N$.

exercise.prompt: Place each number in the smallest displayed domain containing it: $0$, $-5$, $2/3$, $\sqrt2$.
hints: Use the nesting of the four domains.
exercise.solution: $0\in\mathbb N$, $-5\in\mathbb Z$, $2/3\in\mathbb Q$, and $\sqrt2\in\mathbb R$.

sourceRefs.note: Elementary number systems and order.

nodes.title: Operations and precedence
nodes.purpose: Parse an expression unambiguously before computing or rewriting it.
nodes.motivation: Most elementary mistakes are not deep; they come from silently changing the grouping or type of an expression.
nodes.tutorial:
An operation takes input objects and returns an output object. Parentheses state grouping explicitly. Without parentheses, exponentiation is read before multiplication and division, which are read before addition and subtraction; operations at the same level are read from left to right.

Prefer explicit grouping whenever a reader could hesitate. The expression $a/(b+c)$ is different from $a/b+c$, and typography should make that difference impossible to miss.
nodes.keyIdea: Parsing is part of mathematics: preserve grouping before applying any law.

examples.title: Grouping changes value
examples.body: $2(3+4)=14$, while $2\cdot3+4=10$. The parentheses change which operation receives which inputs.

exercise.prompt: Insert parentheses to express 'subtract the product of 3 and 4 from 20', then evaluate it.
hints: Form the product first.

sourceRefs.note: Operation language and order of operations.

nodes.title: Algebraic laws are legal rewrites
nodes.purpose: Replace memorized symbol-moving tricks by named equalities that justify each transformation.
nodes.motivation: Computational algebra and abstract algebra share one core idea: operations obey laws, and those laws license algorithms and rewrites.
nodes.tutorial:
For numbers $a,b,c$ in a domain where the displayed operations are defined, addition and multiplication are associative; both are commutative; and multiplication distributes over addition:

$$a(b+c)=ab+ac.$$

A rewrite is legal when it replaces one side of a known equality by the other within the law's domain. Phrases such as 'move $x$ to the other side' hide the real operation. We instead add or subtract the same value from both sides, multiply both sides by the same value, or divide both sides by the same **nonzero** value. Division by zero is never a legal rewrite.
nodes.keyIdea: A symbolic transformation is an application of a named law, not motion on the page.

examples.title: Expose the law
examples.body: $3(x+2)=3x+6$ follows by distributivity, with $a=3$, $b=x$, and $c=2$.

exercise.prompt: Rewrite $5y+5z$ as a product and name the law used.
hints: Read distributivity in the reverse direction.
exercise.solution: $5y+5z=5(y+z)$ by the distributive law.

sourceRefs.note: Arithmetic properties and equation transformations.
The same law-centered viewpoint scales to algebraic structures.

nodes.title: Equations and solution checking
nodes.purpose: Treat solving as preserving a solution set and verify candidates by substitution.
nodes.motivation: An equation is a statement containing variables. Solving it means finding every allowed substitution that makes the statement true.
nodes.tutorial:
The **solution set** of an equation is the set of domain values that make it true. A reversible operation applied to both sides preserves that set. Some operations, such as squaring, may introduce extra candidates, so the final candidates must be checked in the original equation.

For $2x+3=11$, subtract 3 from both sides and divide both sides by 2 to obtain $x=4$. Substitution checks $2(4)+3=11$.
nodes.keyIdea: Solving preserves truth conditions; checking returns to the original statement.

examples.title: A transparent solution
examples.body: $3x-5=7 \Longleftrightarrow 3x=12 \Longleftrightarrow x=4$. Each arrow is reversible because the same quantity is added to both sides and then both sides are divided by the nonzero number 3.

exercise.prompt: Solve $5x+2=17$ over the real numbers and verify your answer by substitution.
hints: Subtract 2 from both sides, then divide by 5.

sourceRefs.note: Equation solving and solution checking.
Equations as statements with domains.

nodes.title: Inequalities and intervals
nodes.purpose: Describe ordered ranges and solve inequalities without losing the direction of comparison.
nodes.motivation: An equation asks when two quantities meet. An inequality asks which values lie on one side of a boundary, so its answer is usually a whole interval rather than one number.
nodes.tutorial:
The statement $a<b$ places $a$ to the left of $b$ on the real number line. Adding the same real number to both sides preserves the order. Multiplying both sides by a positive number also preserves it. Multiplying by a negative number reverses it, because reflection across zero swaps left and right. Thus $-2x<6$ becomes $x>-3$ after division by $-2$.

Intervals record endpoint choices compactly. A square bracket includes a finite endpoint and a parenthesis excludes it. Infinity is never an endpoint value, so it always receives a parenthesis: $x>-3$ is the interval $(-3,\infty)$.
nodes.keyIdea: An inequality describes a region; a negative scaling reflects that region and reverses its comparison sign.

examples.title: Keep the boundary visible
examples.body: $2x+1\le7$ gives $x\le3$, so the solution set is $(-\infty,3]$. Substituting 3 confirms that the endpoint is included.

exercise.prompt: Solve $5-3x>11$ over the real numbers and write the answer as an interval.
hints: Subtract 5 first.
Dividing by $-3$ reverses the inequality.
exercise.solution: $-3x>6$, hence $x<-2$. The solution interval is $(-\infty,-2)$.

sourceRefs.note: Elementary inequality transformations and interval notation.
Inequalities as statements over an explicit domain.

nodes.title: Statements, truth, and predicates
nodes.purpose: Distinguish a complete true-or-false claim from an expression that still has a free variable.
nodes.motivation: Proof applies to statements. Before proving anything, we must know exactly what claim has a truth value.
nodes.tutorial:
A **statement** is a complete claim that is either true or false. A **predicate** such as $P(x)$ becomes a statement only after $x$ is given a value or bound by a quantifier. For example, '$3$ is even' is a false statement. '$x$ is even' is a predicate whose truth depends on $x$.

Questions, commands, and bare expressions are not statements. The expression $x+1$ denotes an object once $x$ is known; it does not assert anything.
nodes.keyIdea: A proof target must be a complete claim with all variables assigned or quantified.

examples.title: Close the variable
examples.body: $P(x):='x+1>0'$ is a predicate on real numbers. Substituting $x=2$ gives a true statement; substituting $x=-2$ gives a false one.

exercise.prompt: Classify each as statement, predicate, or neither: (a) $2+2=4$; (b) $x^2>0$; (c) $3x+1$.
hints: Ask whether it makes a complete true-or-false claim.
exercise.solution: (a) statement; (b) predicate until a domain and value or quantifier for $x$ are supplied; (c) an expression, so neither.

sourceRefs.note: Statements, open sentences, and truth values.
Friendly introduction to mathematical statements.

nodes.title: Not, and, or
nodes.purpose: Build compound statements with explicit truth conditions.
nodes.motivation: Ordinary language uses 'or' and 'unless' inconsistently. Mathematics needs one stable meaning before arguments can be checked.
nodes.tutorial:
$\neg P$ is true exactly when $P$ is false. $P\land Q$ is true exactly when both statements are true. $P\lor Q$ uses **inclusive or**: it is true when either statement or both statements are true.

These truth conditions are definitions, not stylistic suggestions. More complicated statements can be parsed like expressions: parentheses record which connective acts first.
nodes.keyIdea: Logical connectives are operations on truth values with fixed definitions.

examples.title: Inclusive or
examples.body: The statement '$6$ is even or positive' is true, and both parts happen to be true; mathematical or does not exclude that case.

exercise.prompt: Let $P$ be true and $Q$ be false. Determine the truth values of $\neg P$, $P\land Q$, and $P\lor Q$.
hints: Apply each connective's definition separately.
exercise.solution: $\neg P$ is false, $P\land Q$ is false, and $P\lor Q$ is true.

sourceRefs.note: Propositional connectives and truth tables.
Compound statements and precise negation.

nodes.title: Implication, converse, and if-and-only-if
nodes.purpose: Read one-way and two-way claims without silently reversing them.
nodes.motivation: Confusing a statement with its converse is one of the most common reasoning errors in mathematics and everyday arguments.
nodes.tutorial:
$P\Rightarrow Q$ says that whenever $P$ is true, $Q$ must be true. It does not claim that $Q$ causes $P$, or that $Q\Rightarrow P$. The **converse** is the separately testable statement $Q\Rightarrow P$.

$P\Longleftrightarrow Q$ means both directions hold. In a definition, an if-and-only-if boundary tells us exactly which objects have the defined property.
nodes.keyIdea: An implication has a direction; an equivalence is two implications.

examples.title: A false converse
examples.body: If an integer is divisible by 4, then it is even. The converse is false because 2 is even but not divisible by 4.

exercise.prompt: Write the converse of 'If an integer is a multiple of 6, then it is a multiple of 3,' and decide whether the converse is true.
hints: Swap the hypothesis and conclusion, then search for a counterexample.
exercise.solution: The converse is 'If an integer is a multiple of 3, then it is a multiple of 6.' It is false; 3 is a counterexample.

sourceRefs.note: Implication, converse, and biconditional examples.
Logical form used by later proof methods.

nodes.title: Quantifiers always have domains
nodes.purpose: State whether a claim concerns every object or at least one object, and say where those objects come from.
nodes.motivation: The same words can be true over one domain and false over another. Hidden domains create hidden mistakes.
nodes.tutorial:
$\forall x\in X, P(x)$ says that $P(x)$ holds for every element of $X$. $\exists x\in X, P(x)$ says at least one witness in $X$ makes $P(x)$ true. Write $\exists!x\in X, P(x)$ only when exactly one element works.

To prove a universal statement, work with an arbitrary allowed $x$. To prove an existential statement, provide a specific witness and verify it. A uniqueness claim also requires showing that any two possible witnesses are equal. The order of multiple quantifiers matters: '$\forall x\,\exists y$' may be true even when '$\exists y\,\forall x$' is false.
nodes.keyIdea: A quantifier binds a variable and its domain; changing either changes the statement.

examples.title: Order matters
examples.body: Over the integers, $\forall x\in\mathbb Z,\,\exists y\in\mathbb Z,\ y>x$ is true. But $\exists y\in\mathbb Z,\,\forall x\in\mathbb Z,\ y>x$ is false: no integer exceeds every integer.

exercise.prompt: Over the real numbers, decide whether each statement is true: (a) $\forall x, x^2\ge0$; (b) $\exists x, x^2=-1$.
hints: Use the stated real-number domain.
exercise.solution: (a) true; every real square is nonnegative. (b) false; no real number has square $-1$.

sourceRefs.note: Universal and existential statements with domains.
Quantifier order and witness-based reasoning.

nodes.title: Negating compound statements
nodes.purpose: Produce the exact opposite of a logical claim instead of a vaguely contrary sentence.
nodes.motivation: Contradiction, counterexamples, and error analysis all depend on negating a claim correctly.
nodes.tutorial:
De Morgan's laws exchange and/or under negation:

$$
eg(P\land Q) \Longleftrightarrow (
eg P)\lor(
eg Q),$$
$$
eg(P\lor Q) \Longleftrightarrow (
eg P)\land(
eg Q).$$

Quantifiers also exchange: the negation of 'every $x$ works' is 'some $x$ fails,' and the negation of 'some $x$ works' is 'every $x$ fails.' Formally, $
eg orall x\,P(x)\Longleftrightarrow\exists x\,
eg P(x)$.
nodes.keyIdea: Negation crosses one logical layer at a time, switching and/or and every/some.

examples.title: Negate a universal
examples.body: The negation of 'Every integer is even' is 'There exists an integer that is not even,' not 'Every integer is odd.'

exercise.prompt: Negate: 'For every real number $x$, $x>0$ or $x=0$.'
hints: Switch every to there exists, then negate the or.
exercise.solution: There exists a real number $x$ such that $x\le0$ and $x\ne0$; equivalently, there exists a real number $x<0$.

sourceRefs.note: Negations of quantified and compound statements.
Logical equivalences and De Morgan's laws.

nodes.proofGoal: Derive the correct negation of a quantified compound claim and justify each logical switch.

nodes.title: Direct proof and explicit witnesses
nodes.purpose: Turn a quantified claim into a short sequence of checkable obligations.
nodes.motivation: A proof is not a report that examples worked. It must explain why the conclusion follows for an arbitrary allowed input, or exhibit and verify the object promised by an existence claim.
nodes.tutorial:
For a universal implication $\forall x\in X, P(x)\Rightarrow Q(x)$, begin with an arbitrary $x\in X$, assume $P(x)$, and use definitions or established laws until $Q(x)$ follows. The word **arbitrary** matters: the argument may not rely on a special feature of one convenient example.

For an existential claim $\exists x\in X, P(x)$, choose a specific witness $w\in X$ and verify $P(w)$. The choice and the verification are separate proof steps.
nodes.keyIdea: Universal proofs keep the input arbitrary; existential proofs name and check a witness.

examples.title: Unpack a definition
examples.body: Suppose an integer $n$ is a multiple of 6, so $n=6k$ for some integer $k$. Since $n=3(2k)$ and $2k$ is an integer, $n$ is a multiple of 3.

examples.title: Give a witness
examples.body: To prove that an integer with square 49 exists, choose $w:=7$. It is an integer and $w^2=49$.

exercise.prompt: Prove: for every integer $n$, if $n$ is a multiple of 10, then $n$ is a multiple of 5.
hints: Write the hypothesis as $n=10k$ for an integer $k$.
Rewrite 10 as $5\cdot2$.
exercise.solution: Let $n$ be an arbitrary integer and suppose $n=10k$ for some integer $k$. Then $n=5(2k)$. Because $2k$ is an integer, the definition of multiple shows that $n$ is a multiple of 5.

sourceRefs.note: Direct proof structure and witness-based existence proofs.
Proofs of universal implications from definitions.
Checkable proof steps and explicit witnesses.

nodes.proofGoal: Construct a direct proof from an arbitrary input or prove an existence claim by naming and verifying a witness.

nodes.title: Counterexamples and disproof
nodes.purpose: Refute a universal claim with one relevant object while recognizing that examples alone do not establish universality.
nodes.motivation: A single failure can settle a universal claim, but only when the example belongs to the stated domain and actually violates the stated conclusion.
nodes.tutorial:
The negation of $\forall x\in X, P(x)$ is $\exists x\in X, \neg P(x)$. A **counterexample** is exactly such a witness: an allowed object $c$ for which the claimed property fails. A complete disproof therefore checks both $c\in X$ and $\neg P(c)$.

Ten successful tests do not prove a universal statement, because an untested input may still fail. One verified counterexample does disprove it.
nodes.keyIdea: A counterexample is a witness to the precise negation of a universal statement.

examples.title: Cross terms matter
examples.body: The claim $(a+b)^2=a^2+b^2$ for all real $a,b$ fails at $a=b=1$: the left side is 4 and the right side is 2.

exercise.prompt: Disprove: for every real number $x$, $(x-1)(x+1)=x^2+1$.
hints: Try $x=0$.
Evaluate both sides separately.
exercise.solution: Choose $x:=0$. It is real, and the left side is $(-1)(1)=-1$ while the right side is $0^2+1=1$. Since the values differ, the universal identity is false.

sourceRefs.note: Counterexamples as a response to universal claims.
Disproof by a checked counterexample.

nodes.proofGoal: Disprove a universal claim by giving an in-domain counterexample and verifying the exact failure.

nodes.title: Proof by cases
nodes.purpose: Split an argument into possibilities that together cover every allowed input.
nodes.motivation: Some hypotheses naturally offer several routes. A case proof is sound only when no possible input falls between the routes.
nodes.tutorial:
To prove $Q$ from a disjunction $P_1\lor P_2$, prove $Q$ assuming $P_1$, prove $Q$ assuming $P_2$, and state why the two cases exhaust the hypothesis. Cases may overlap; they must cover everything.

A useful case split is chosen from the structure of the problem, not from a desire to list examples. For ordered real numbers, a hypothesis such as $x\le-1$ or $x\ge1$ already supplies two complete cases.
nodes.keyIdea: Each case proves the same target, and the cases together leave no allowed input untreated.

examples.title: Two sides of an interval
examples.body: If $x\le-1$, then both $x-1$ and $x+1$ are nonpositive, so their product is nonnegative. If $x\ge1$, both are nonnegative. Hence $(x-1)(x+1)\ge0$ whenever $x\le-1$ or $x\ge1$.

exercise.prompt: Prove that $x^2\ge1$ for every real $x$ satisfying $x\le-1$ or $x\ge1$.
hints: Handle the two alternatives separately.
In either case, compare the absolute size of $x$ with 1 without introducing new notation.
exercise.solution: Let $x$ satisfy the hypothesis. If $x\ge1$, multiplying $x\ge1$ by the nonnegative number $x$ gives $x^2\ge x\ge1$. If $x\le-1$, then $-x\ge1$; multiplying by the nonnegative number $-x$ gives $(-x)^2\ge-x\ge1$, and $(-x)^2=x^2$. The two stated cases exhaust the hypothesis.

sourceRefs.note: Case-based proof organization.
Exhaustive cases as a proof pattern.

nodes.proofGoal: Prove one conclusion in every case of an explicit exhaustive split.

nodes.title: Indirect proof
nodes.purpose: Use contraposition or contradiction when assuming failure exposes the useful structure.
nodes.motivation: Some conclusions reveal little when approached directly. Their negations can force a concrete equation, missing witness, or impossible bound.
nodes.tutorial:
To prove $P\Rightarrow Q$ by **contraposition**, prove the equivalent implication $\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$. To prove a statement by **contradiction**, assume its negation and derive an impossibility: two incompatible claims, or a violation of a definition or established law.

An indirect proof must name the assumption being negated and identify the exact contradiction. The symbol $\bot$ may mark that endpoint, but the prose must say what conflicts.
nodes.keyIdea: Indirect proof assumes the target fails and follows that assumption to a checkable impossibility.

examples.title: No greatest integer
examples.body: Assume an integer $g$ is greatest. Then $g+1$ is also an integer and $g+1>g$, contradicting the defining claim that no integer is larger than $g$.

exercise.prompt: Prove by contraposition: for every real $x$, if $x^2<4$, then $-2<x<2$.
hints: Negating $-2<x<2$ gives $x\le-2$ or $x\ge2$.
Use cases to show either alternative implies $x^2\ge4$.
exercise.solution: We prove the contrapositive. Suppose $x\le-2$ or $x\ge2$. If $x\ge2$, multiplying by the nonnegative $x$ gives $x^2\ge2x\ge4$. If $x\le-2$, then $-x\ge2$, so $x^2=(-x)^2\ge2(-x)\ge4$. Thus not $(-2<x<2)$ implies $x^2\ge4$, proving the original implication by contraposition.

sourceRefs.note: Contrapositive and contradiction proof forms.
Logical justification for indirect arguments.
Contradiction with an explicitly identified impossible conclusion.

nodes.proofGoal: Prove a claim by stating its contrapositive or negation and deriving the required opposite conclusion or an explicit contradiction.

nodes.title: Mathematical induction
nodes.purpose: Prove a claim for every natural number by establishing a starting point and a successor step.
nodes.motivation: An infinite list of separate checks is impossible. Induction packages them into one initial verification and one reusable step.
nodes.tutorial:
Let $P(n)$ be a statement for $n\in\mathbb N$. An induction proof has two obligations. The **base case** proves $P(0)$. The **inductive step** fixes an arbitrary $n\in\mathbb N$, assumes $P(n)$ as the induction hypothesis, and proves $P(n+1)$.

The step is conditional: it does not assume the theorem for every number at once. It shows that whenever the claim has reached one natural number, it reaches the next. If a theorem starts at 1 or another index, state that base explicitly.
nodes.keyIdea: Base case plus successor step covers the natural numbers from the stated starting index onward.

examples.title: Track the hypothesis
examples.body: For $P(n): 1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^2$ with $n\ge1$, adding the next odd number $2n+1$ turns $n^2$ into $n^2+2n+1=(n+1)^2$.

exercise.prompt: Use induction to prove $2^n\ge n+1$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$.
hints: At $n=0$, compare 1 with 1.
In the step, double the induction hypothesis and compare $2n+2$ with $n+2$.
exercise.solution: Base: $2^0=1\ge1$. Step: assume $2^n\ge n+1$ for an arbitrary $n\in\mathbb N$. Then $2^{n+1}=2\cdot2^n\ge2(n+1)=2n+2\ge n+2$, since $n\ge0$. Thus $P(n+1)$ holds, so induction proves the claim for all natural numbers.

sourceRefs.note: Induction as a base case and successor implication.

nodes.proofGoal: Prove a natural-number claim by verifying the declared base case and an inductive step that explicitly uses the induction hypothesis.

nodes.title: Set-builder notation
nodes.purpose: Define a set by a domain and one precise membership condition.
nodes.motivation: Lists work for tiny finite sets. Most mathematical sets need a rule that states exactly which objects belong.
nodes.tutorial:
The expression $\{x\in X:P(x)\}$ means the set of elements $x$ from the ambient domain $X$ for which $P(x)$ is true. The domain comes first; the membership test comes after the colon.

NisabaDB uses a colon rather than a vertical bar. Both are common, but the vertical bar is already used for divisibility, conditional probability, and restrictions in later subjects.
nodes.keyIdea: A set-builder expression is a filter: domain in, predicate applied, satisfying elements out.

examples.title: Even natural numbers
examples.body: $E:=\{n\in\mathbb N: \exists k\in\mathbb N, n=2k\}$ defines the even natural numbers without an endless list.

exercise.prompt: Write the set of negative real numbers in NisabaDB's set-builder notation.
hints: State the real-number domain before the colon.
exercise.solution: $\{x\in\mathbb R:x<0\}$.

sourceRefs.note: Roster and set-builder forms.
Set-builder notation reused in algebraic structures.

nodes.title: Subsets without ambiguity
nodes.purpose: Express containment with separate symbols for inclusive and strict containment.
nodes.motivation: The symbol $\subset$ means inclusive subset in some books and proper subset in others. A unified textbook cannot inherit both conventions.
nodes.tutorial:
$A\subseteq B$ means every element of $A$ belongs to $B$:

$$A\subseteq B \Longleftrightarrow \forall x\in A,\ x\in B.$$

Equality is allowed. Write $A\subsetneq B$ when $A\subseteq B$ and $A\ne B$. NisabaDB never uses bare $\subset$ because its meaning is not stable across sources.
nodes.keyIdea: $\subseteq$ allows equality; $\subsetneq$ requires a missing element.

examples.title: Inclusive and proper
examples.body: $\{1,2\}\subseteq\{1,2\}$ is true. Also $\{1\}\subsetneq\{1,2\}$ because 2 belongs only to the larger set.

exercise.prompt: Let $A=\{1,2\}$ and $B=\{1,2,3\}$. Decide the truth of $A\subseteq B$, $B\subseteq A$, and $A\subsetneq B$.
hints: Check each element and then check equality.
exercise.solution: $A\subseteq B$ and $A\subsetneq B$ are true. $B\subseteq A$ is false because $3\in B$ but $3\notin A$.

sourceRefs.note: Subset definitions and element proofs.
Source comparison for inclusive/proper notation.
Containment notation used by later algebra chapters.

nodes.title: Union, intersection, and difference
nodes.purpose: Build new sets with operations whose membership rules are just logical connectives.
nodes.motivation: Set operations look like a new subject, but their definitions are the logic of membership. This is a major redundancy we can remove.
nodes.keyIdea: Union is or, intersection is and, and difference is and-not applied to membership.

exercise.prompt: Let $U=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, $A=\{2,4,6\}$, and $B=\{4,5,6\}$. Compute $A\cup B$, $A\cap B$, $A\setminus B$, and $U\setminus A$.
hints: For union, keep elements occurring in at least one set.
For difference, begin in the set named on the left.

nodes.title: Power sets
nodes.purpose: Collect all subsets of one set into a new set whose elements are themselves sets.
nodes.motivation: Mathematics often needs to choose or compare possible subcollections. A power set turns those choices into ordinary elements of one larger collection.
nodes.tutorial:
The **power set** of $A$ is

$$\mathcal{P}(A):=\{S:S\subseteq A\},$$

where the variable $S$ ranges over sets. Its elements are subsets, not the original elements of $A$. The **empty set** $\varnothing$ is the set with no elements. It belongs to every power set because $\varnothing\subseteq A$, and $A$ itself belongs because $A\subseteq A$. Do not confuse $a\in A$ with $\{a\}\in\mathcal{P}(A)$: the first relates an object to $A$, while the second treats a singleton set as an element of the power set.
nodes.keyIdea: Elements of $\mathcal{P}(A)$ are sets selected from $A$.

examples.title: A two-element base set
examples.body: If $A=\{a,b\}$, then $\mathcal{P}(A)=\{\varnothing,\{a\},\{b\},\{a,b\}\}$.

exercise.prompt: List $\mathcal{P}(\{1,2,3\})$ and explain why 1 is not one of its elements.
hints: Organize the subsets by size: zero, one, two, and three elements.
A power-set element must itself be a set.
exercise.solution: $\mathcal{P}(\{1,2,3\})=\{\varnothing,\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{1,2,3\}\}$. The number 1 is not a set selected from $A$; the singleton $\{1\}$ is the corresponding power-set element.

sourceRefs.note: Power-set notation and finite examples.

nodes.title: Ordered pairs and Cartesian products
nodes.purpose: Represent two-coordinate data whose first and second positions have different roles.
nodes.motivation: A set forgets order, but an input-output record, a grid location, or a directed edge must remember which entry comes first.
nodes.tutorial:
An **ordered pair** $(a,b)$ has a first coordinate $a$ and a second coordinate $b$. Two ordered pairs are equal exactly when corresponding coordinates agree: $(a,b)=(c,d)$ precisely when $a=c$ and $b=d$. Usually $(a,b)\ne(b,a)$.

The Cartesian product is

$$A\times B:=\{(a,b):a\in A\text{ and }b\in B\}.$$

NisabaDB reserves $\times$ for Cartesian products and uses $\cdot$ when multiplication needs an explicit symbol.
nodes.keyIdea: A Cartesian product lists every allowed first-coordinate and second-coordinate combination, with order preserved.

examples.title: A small product
examples.body: $\{r,b\}\times\{0,1\}=\{(r,0),(r,1),(b,0),(b,1)\}$. Reversing the factors produces pairs with a number first and a letter second.

exercise.prompt: Let $A=\{1,2\}$ and $B=\{x,y,z\}$. List $A\times B$ and $B\times A$.
hints: Hold one first coordinate fixed while cycling through the second set.
The two products have the same size but usually different elements.

sourceRefs.note: Ordered-pair equality and Cartesian products.

nodes.title: Set identities by following an element
nodes.purpose: Prove two constructed sets equal by translating membership into logic and back again.
nodes.motivation: A diagram can suggest a set identity, but extensionality and logic explain why it holds for every choice of sets.
nodes.tutorial:
Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of a universe $U$. De Morgan's set identity is

$$U\setminus(A\cup B)=(U\setminus A)\cap(U\setminus B).$$

Take an arbitrary $x\in U$. Membership on the left means $x\notin A\cup B$, which means it is not true that $x\in A$ or $x\in B$. Logical De Morgan changes this to $x\notin A$ and $x\notin B$. That is exactly membership in the right side. Because the two membership conditions agree for every $x\in U$, extensionality gives equality.
nodes.keyIdea: For a set identity, reduce both sides to equivalent statements about one arbitrary element.

examples.title: Element-chasing template
examples.body: A clean proof has the form $x\in L\Longleftrightarrow$ a logical condition $\Longleftrightarrow x\in R$, followed by one sentence invoking extensionality.

exercise.prompt: Prove $A\setminus(B\cup C)=(A\setminus B)\cap(A\setminus C)$ for subsets $A,B,C$ of a universe $U$.
hints: Begin with an arbitrary $x\in U$.
Translate difference as 'in the first set and not in the second,' then apply logical De Morgan.
exercise.solution:
For arbitrary $x\in U$, $x\in A\setminus(B\cup C)$ iff $x\in A$ and $x
otin B\cup C$. This holds iff $x\in A$, $x
otin B$, and $x
otin C$, which is equivalent to $x\in A\setminus B$ and $x\in A\setminus C$. Thus $x\in(A\setminus B)\cap(A\setminus C)$. Extensionality proves the identity.

nodes.proofGoal: Prove a set identity by translating membership in each side into the same logical condition for an arbitrary element.

nodes.title: Functions, domains, and codomains
nodes.purpose: Treat a function as a typed assignment with exactly one output for every allowed input.
nodes.motivation: A formula is not a complete function until its allowed inputs and promised output set are known. Those types decide whether the rule is total, whether it is onto, and whether two functions are equal.
nodes.tutorial:
A function declaration $f:A\to B$ names the **domain** $A$ and **codomain** $B$. For every $x\in A$, there must be exactly one value $f(x)\in B$. The notation $x\mapsto f(x)$ describes the assignment; it does not replace the typed declaration.

In this textbook, two functions are equal when they have the same domain, the same codomain, and the same value at every input. A rule that misses an allowed input or offers two outputs for one input is not a function with the claimed type.
nodes.keyIdea: A function is a complete, single-valued assignment from a declared domain to a declared codomain.

examples.title: A finite typed function
examples.body: Let $A=\{r,b,g\}$ and $B=\{\text{circle},\text{square}\}$. The assignments $f(r)=\text{circle}$, $f(b)=\text{square}$, and $f(g)=\text{circle}$ define a function $f:A\to B$. Each element of $A$ receives exactly one element of $B$; outputs are allowed to repeat.

exercise.prompt: Let $A=\{a,b,c\}$ and $B=\{u,v\}$. Does the proposed assignment $\{(a,u),(b,u),(b,v)\}$ define a function $A\to B$? Explain both failures.
hints: Check whether every element of $A$ appears as a first coordinate.
Check whether any first coordinate is paired with two outputs.
exercise.solution: No. The input $c$ has no assigned output, so the assignment is not total on $A$. The input $b$ is paired with both $u$ and $v$, so the assignment is not single-valued. Either failure is enough to prevent a function $A\to B$.

sourceRefs.note: Functions with explicit domains, codomains, and output uniqueness.

nodes.title: Images and preimages
nodes.purpose: Move whole sets forward or backward through a function without pretending that the function is invertible.
nodes.motivation: Many questions concern all outputs from a region or all inputs reaching a target region. These operations are defined for every function, including functions that merge inputs or miss outputs.
nodes.tutorial:
Let $f:A\to B$, $S\subseteq A$, and $T\subseteq B$. The **image** of $S$ is

$$f[S]:=\{y\in B:\exists x\in S, y=f(x)\}.$$

The **preimage** of $T$ is

$$f^{-1}[T]:=\{x\in A:f(x)\in T\}.$$

Brackets signal that the input is a set. The preimage notation does not assert that an inverse function exists; it simply filters the domain by where $f$ lands.
nodes.keyIdea: Images collect reached outputs; preimages collect inputs that reach a chosen target set.

examples.title: A many-to-one function
examples.body: For $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=x^2$, we have $f[\{-2,1\}]=\{1,4\}$ and $f^{-1}[\{1,4\}]=\{-2,-1,1,2\}$. The preimage is meaningful even though $f$ is not one-to-one.

exercise.prompt: For $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ defined by $f(n)=2n$, compute $f[\{-1,0,2\}]$ and $f^{-1}[\{0,4\}]$.
hints: For the image, evaluate each listed input.
For the preimage, solve $2n=0$ and $2n=4$ in the integer domain.

sourceRefs.note: Images and inverse images of subsets.

nodes.title: Composition and identity functions
nodes.purpose: Combine compatible functions in the correct order and recognize the function that changes nothing.
nodes.motivation: Long mathematical constructions are assembled from shorter maps. Their types determine which outputs may legally become the next inputs.
nodes.tutorial:
If $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$, their composition is the function $g\circ f:A\to C$ defined by

$$(g\circ f)(x):=g(f(x)).$$

Read $g\circ f$ as '$g$ after $f$': the right-hand function acts first. The identity function on $A$ is $\operatorname{id}_A:A\to A$, defined by $\operatorname{id}_A(x):=x$. It satisfies $f\circ\operatorname{id}_A=f$ and $\operatorname{id}_B\circ f=f$. Composition is associative because both parenthesizations send $x$ to the same final value.
nodes.keyIdea: Composition follows the flow of types from right to left; identity leaves every input unchanged.

examples.title: Order changes the rule
examples.body: For $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=x^2$, $(g\circ f)(x)=(x+1)^2$, while $(f\circ g)(x)=x^2+1$.

exercise.prompt: Using $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=x^2$ on the real numbers, compute $(g\circ f)(3)$ and $(f\circ g)(3)$, then verify one identity-function equation at 3.
hints: Apply the function nearest the input first.
$\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R}(3)=3$.
exercise.solution: $(g\circ f)(3)=g(4)=16$ and $(f\circ g)(3)=f(9)=10$. Also $(f\circ\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R})(3)=f(3)=4$, which agrees with the identity law.

sourceRefs.note: Composition, identity maps, and type compatibility.

nodes.title: Injective, surjective, and bijective functions
nodes.purpose: Separate loss of input information from failure to reach the whole codomain.
nodes.motivation: Two functions with the same formula can have different structural properties when their domains or codomains change. The definitions must therefore mention the declared type.
nodes.tutorial:
A function $f:A\to B$ is **injective** when equal outputs force equal inputs:

$$\forall x_1,x_2\in A,\quad f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow x_1=x_2.$$

It is **surjective** when every codomain element is reached:

$$\forall y\in B,\quad\exists x\in A,\ f(x)=y.$$

It is **bijective** when both properties hold. To disprove injectivity, exhibit two distinct inputs with one output. To disprove surjectivity, exhibit a codomain value with no preimage.
nodes.keyIdea: Injective means no collisions; surjective means no missed codomain values; bijective means both.

examples.title: The codomain matters
examples.body: $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$, $f(n)=2n$, is injective but not surjective because no integer maps to 1. The map $g:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$, $g(n)=n+1$, is bijective.

exercise.prompt: Classify $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $q(x)=x^2$, as injective, surjective, both, or neither. Give explicit witnesses for each failure.
hints: Compare the inputs 1 and $-1$.
Ask whether any real input can map to $-1$.
exercise.solution: $q$ is neither. It is not injective because $q(1)=q(-1)=1$ while $1\ne-1$. It is not surjective because the codomain value $-1$ is not the square of any real number.

nodes.title: A function is invertible exactly when it is bijective
nodes.purpose: Characterize when a function can be undone in both directions and show that the undoing function is unique.
nodes.motivation: The symbol $f^{-1}$ is often written too early. The bijection theorem states the exact condition that earns the right to use it for a function.
nodes.tutorial:
An inverse of $f:A\to B$ is a function $h:B\to A$ satisfying

$$h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_A\quad\text{and}\quad f\circ h=\operatorname{id}_B.$$

If such $h$ exists, equal outputs of $f$ can be sent through $h$ to recover equal inputs, so $f$ is injective. For every $y\in B$, choosing $x:=h(y)$ gives $f(x)=y$, so $f$ is surjective. Conversely, if $f$ is bijective, each $y\in B$ has exactly one input $x\in A$ with $f(x)=y$; define $f^{-1}(y)$ to be that input. The two identity equations follow. Any two inverses must give that same unique input, so the inverse is unique.
nodes.keyIdea: A two-sided inverse exists precisely when every codomain value comes from one and only one domain value.

examples.title: Undo an affine function
examples.body: For $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=3x-2$, solving $y=3x-2$ for $x$ gives $f^{-1}(y)=(y+2)/3$. Substitution in both composition orders returns the input.

exercise.prompt: Suppose $h,k:B\to A$ are both inverses of $f:A\to B$. Prove that $h=k$.
hints: Start with an arbitrary $y\in B$.
Use $f(k(y))=y$, then use $h(f(x))=x$.
exercise.solution: Let $y\in B$ be arbitrary. Because $k$ is an inverse, $f(k(y))=y$. Therefore $h(y)=h(f(k(y)))=k(y)$ because $h\circ f=\operatorname{id}_A$. Thus $h$ and $k$ agree at every $y\in B$, and they have the same domain and codomain, so $h=k$.
